name: Daria Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a mixed family farm, forty hectares, with about eighty ewes, a dozen beef cattle, a big vegetable patch and some laying hens, and we sell most of it through our own farm shop by the road. My husband Ben looks after the animals, and I run the shop and the veg. A normal day for me is picking for the shop at seven, opening at nine, then serving, ordering, doing the meat boxes and posting on the shop's page in between.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the regulars. There's a retired teacher, Mr Okafor, who comes every Friday for two lamb chops and twenty minutes of talk about his roses. What wears me out is the margin. We sell good food at a fair price, and after the butcher, the electric for the fridges and the card machine fees, there's very little left.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Loads, every day. I use an AI assistant to write the shop posts, plan the veg so we don't all have courgettes at once, and work out the staff rota for the Saturday girls. Ben thinks I'm married to my phone, and he's not entirely wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the next five years, one at a time. Here's the first. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's brilliant for small businesses and I'd tell anyone who'd listen. I've already shown two other farm shops how I use it for posts and stock lists. I'd probably post about that, to be honest, the shop's page does well when I talk about how we work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's useful, but it won't fix the fact that supermarkets sell eggs cheaper than I can buy the feed for. It saves me two hours a week, maybe. That's nice, but it doesn't pay the electric.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it and try a few more tricks, like using it to answer the online orders faster. I'd look at whether I could sell meat boxes further away with better posts, maybe in the first three months. I wouldn't spend much, there's maybe a month's float in the shop account at the best of times, often less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, a bit keen. It's a better tool, that's all, and I like tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shop account is often less than a month. What does a bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: January. Nobody buys anything after Christmas, the fridges still run, and the Saturday girls still need paying. Last January I paid the butcher late for the first time in eleven years, and I hated ringing him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd show other shops how to use it. Aren't they competition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The nearest one is fifteen miles away, and we're all fighting the same supermarket. If farm shops get better, people get in the habit of using them, and that helps me too.

S0.say: I'd say AI is brilliant for small businesses, and I've already shown two other farm shops how I use it. I'd post about how we work, because those posts do well.
S0.think: I really think it's useful but won't fix supermarkets selling eggs cheaper than my feed costs. It saves me two hours a week, which doesn't pay the electric.
S0.do: Keeps using AI and tries it for faster replies to online orders. Tests selling meat boxes further afield with better posts within three months, without spending much from a float that's often under a month.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit keen, because she likes good tools.
S0.quote: It saves me two hours a week, maybe. That's nice, but it doesn't pay the electric.
S0.fieldNote: She's a confident daily AI user who shares tips with other farm shops instead of guarding them. The shop's thin margin is the real pressure, and paying the butcher late hurt her pride. She treats AI as useful but not a rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change gives small businesses like ours a chance to keep up. I'd keep saying try it, because it costs nothing to try. And I'd say farm shops should band together and share what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed. I'd want it faster because I'm already ahead with it and that gives me an edge. Fewer beginners worries me, though, because the Saturday girls are my beginners and they'll need somewhere to go next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep pushing ahead. I'd try an AI tool for planning what to plant next year based on what sold, maybe by spring. I'd also start a small network with three or four other farm shops, so we can share an online ordering system and split the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keen, with a small worry about the girls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the Saturday girls.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Priya and Hannah, both seventeen, both saving for university. Priya's brilliant on the till and she's learned to talk to the old customers, which you can't teach. If the bigger shops hire fewer like her, she'll miss out on the first job that teaches you how to deal with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're ahead and it gives you an edge. Is there a part of you that likes it being slow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, honestly. If it's slow, I stay ahead for longer. That's not a nice thing to say, but it's true.

S1.say: I'd say slow change gives small businesses a chance to keep up, and I'd keep telling people to try it. Farm shops should band together and share what works.
S1.think: I'm privately a bit disappointed, because I'm ahead and faster change would give me an edge. Fewer beginners worries me for my Saturday staff.
S1.do: Tries an AI tool by spring to plan next year's planting from sales. Starts a network with three or four farm shops to share an online ordering system and split the cost.
S1.feel: Keen, with a small worry about the Saturday girls.
S1.quote: If it's slow, I stay ahead for longer. That's not a nice thing to say, but it's true.
S1.fieldNote: She admitted she'd quietly enjoy staying ahead of slower competitors, a frank moment. Her Saturday staff, Priya and Hannah, stand in for the beginners she worries about. Sharing costs with other farm shops is her instinctive move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is hard on office workers and the government needs a plan, but not one that blocks new things. I'd say there are new jobs if people are willing to learn. I'd say that on the shop page, gently, because half my customers work in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it could be good for the shop and bad for my customers. People who lose office jobs might have time to cook and want proper food, but less money for it. My meat boxes are a treat, and treats are the first thing you cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI to plan cheaper boxes in the first couple of months, a family box with the cheaper cuts and seasonal veg. I'd offer a small discount for people who've lost their jobs, quietly. And I'd look at running cooking evenings in the barn, because people with time on their hands want something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a list of ideas, which is how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A discount for people who lost jobs. How would you know who they are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just trust them. If you've lost your job and you're buying mince at my shop instead of the supermarket, you're the kind of customer I want. Some might take advantage, but most people round here wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ben make of the cooking evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He groaned and said he'd have to tidy the barn. But he'd do it, and he'd end up telling everyone how to bone a shoulder of lamb. He's shy until he's talking about his sheep.

S2.say: I'd say it's hard on office workers and the government needs a plan, but not one that blocks new things. I'd gently say on the shop page that new jobs exist for people willing to learn.
S2.think: I really think it could help the shop and hurt my customers. Office workers might cook more but have less money, and meat boxes are a treat people cut first.
S2.do: Uses AI to design a cheaper family box with cheaper cuts and seasonal veg within two months. Quietly offers a discount to people who've lost jobs and plans cooking evenings in the barn.
S2.feel: Uneasy, but coping by making a list of ideas.
S2.quote: If you've lost your job and you're buying mince at my shop instead of the supermarket, you're the kind of customer I want.
S2.fieldNote: She thinks like a shopkeeper first, reading the picture through her customers' wallets. Her answer to worry is a list of ideas. Her centre politics show in wanting a plan that helps people without blocking new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared fairly, with help for people who lose jobs, but I'd not side with either lot shouting. I'd say buy local, keep the money here. I'd say that on the shop page and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's mixed. Rich people with share money moving out to the country would buy expensive boxes, and I'd do well with them. But my old regulars, like Mr Okafor on his pension, might get priced out of the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI to set up a premium box for the new money, maybe in the first three months, and charge properly for it. I'd use that to keep a cheaper box going for the regulars. I'd also look at a small loan to add a café corner, since the house boom would bring more people past the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit guilty, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be doing well out of a crisis that's hurting a lot of people. I'd be selling rib of beef to a man with a big share payout while someone else lost their career. I'd keep the cheap box going partly to feel better about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan on a thin cushion is a risk. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and Ben would make me think about it more. I'd keep it small, maybe five thousand, and only if the first three months of premium boxes paid. If they didn't, no café, simple as that.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should be shared fairly with help for people who lose jobs, without siding with either lot shouting. I'd tell people on the shop page to buy local and keep money here.
S3.think: I really think it's mixed: newly rich people moving out would buy expensive boxes and I'd do well. But regulars like Mr Okafor on a pension might be priced out.
S3.do: Uses AI to set up a premium box for new money within three months and uses its profit to keep a cheaper box for regulars. Considers a small loan of about five thousand for a café corner, only if the premium boxes pay.
S3.feel: Excited and a bit guilty at the same time.
S3.quote: I'd be selling rib of beef to a man with a big share payout while someone else lost their career.
S3.fieldNote: She's the rare persona who'd do well from the fast picture, and she feels guilty about it. She uses the premium box to fund a cheap one for her regulars. She'd only take a loan if the first three months proved it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will still want real food grown by real people, and that's where small farms can win. I'd say the government should help small farms adapt, not just protect the big ones. I'd say it on the page and probably make it the shop's motto.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think robots in warehouses and kitchens would make supermarket food even cheaper. My best-selling thing isn't the sausages. It's me behind the till knowing your name. A robot can't sell that, but it can make everyone else cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean hard on being the human shop, real people, real names, the cooking evenings, the story of each animal. I'd look at a cheap robot for the veg weeding, if one came out at a few thousand, maybe in the second year once I'd seen reviews. And I'd keep the Saturday girls, because they're part of what people pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but fired up. It's the biggest fight the shop's ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a weeding robot but keep the girls. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, because nobody comes to the shop to watch me weed. They come to chat at the till. I'd give the boring bit to the machine and keep the bits that people love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if being the human shop isn't enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd shrink it right down to the meat boxes and the regulars, and Ben would go back to just sheep. I'd rather do it small and properly than chase the supermarkets. But I'd give it a real go first.

S4.say: I'd say people will still want real food grown by real people, and that's where small farms win. Government should help small farms adapt, not just protect the big ones.
S4.think: I really think warehouse and kitchen robots would make supermarket food cheaper still. My shop's real selling point is me knowing customers' names, which a robot can't copy.
S4.do: Leans hard on being the human shop, with names, cooking evenings and the story of each animal. Buys a cheap weeding robot in year two if one comes out at a few thousand, and keeps the Saturday staff.
S4.feel: Anxious but fired up, facing the biggest fight the shop has had.
S4.quote: My best-selling thing isn't the sausages. It's me behind the till knowing your name.
S4.fieldNote: She sees the human touch as her product, so she'd automate the weeding but not the till. Her fallback is to shrink to the regulars rather than chase supermarket prices. She stayed hopeful and ready to fight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because that's when the supermarkets get so cheap that people stop caring where their food comes from. What would help is something that helps small farm shops get noticed, local food schemes, maybe schools and hospitals buying from farms like ours. And a small grant for the tools, not a loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the regulars, and they're the whole thing. If Mr Okafor stops coming because the village changes, I'll miss him more than the money. A farm shop is half food and half company.

headlineQuote: My best-selling thing isn't the sausages. It's me behind the till knowing your name. A robot can't sell that, but it can make everyone else cheaper.
portrait: Daria is 58 and runs the farm shop and vegetables on a forty-hectare mixed family farm, while her husband Ben keeps the sheep and cattle. She uses an AI assistant every day for posts, planting plans and rotas, and shares tips with other farm shops. She reads every picture through her customers: office job losses mean cheaper boxes, the share boom brings rich buyers she feels guilty about serving, and robots make the supermarket even cheaper. Her answer is to sell what a robot can't, a person behind the till who knows your name.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, because supermarket food would get so cheap that people stop caring where their food comes from.
whatWouldHelp: Local food schemes, such as schools and hospitals buying from farms like hers, and small grants for tools instead of loans.
